title: Why Authorization Fails
subtitle: Authentication vs authorization, and the cost of if-statements
content:
🔐 Authentication Is Not Authorization

Authentication (AuthN) answers who are you? — passwords, SSO, JWTs, API keys. Authorization (AuthZ) answers what may you do? — can this identity read this report, edit this tenant, see this column?

The industry failure mode: teams invest heavily in AuthN (OIDC, MFA, Keycloak) and then scatter AuthZ as if user.role == "admin" checks across every service. Those checks are untestable as a whole, unauditable, and drift between services until a breach finds the gap.

💥 Three Real Breach Shapes

  • Broken object-level authorization (BOLA/IDOR): GET /invoices/1234 returns any invoice when the id is guessed, because the handler checks login but never checks ownership. OWASP API #1 year after year.
  • Tenant leakage: an analyst for tenant A reads tenant B's rows because the query forgot WHERE tenant_id = ?. One missing predicate, full cross-customer exposure.
  • Fail-open defaults: an authorizer that returns ALLOW when the policy engine is unreachable, misconfigured, or the input shape is unexpected. Deny must be the default.

📜 Policy-Based Access Control in One Paragraph

PBAC externalizes authorization decisions into versioned, testable policies evaluated by a dedicated policy decision point (PDP) at request time. Application code asks may S do A on R given context C? and enforces the answer — it never hard-codes the answer. Policies live in Git, go through review, run in CI, and ship like code.

🧭 What This Course Covers

  • Foundations (L1): models compared, architecture, default-deny, business case
  • Languages (L2): OPA/Rego, Cedar, OpenFGA — hands-on, critically reviewed against official docs and real-world repos
  • Platforms (L3): OPA/Cedar/OpenFGA in production, plus Immuta (data) and PlainID (enterprise) scenarios
  • Architecture (L4): enforcement patterns, testing, RBAC-to-PBAC migration
  • Capstones (L5): AI-agent guardrails and two build-and-defend projects with rubrics

✅ How to Use This Course

Each lesson has written content, a Policy Lab visualizer on the right, and a 5-question knowledge check (60% to pass). Lessons unlock sequentially. Your progress saves in the browser automatically.

questions.question: What is the core difference between authentication and authorization?

options.text: Authentication proves who you are; authorization decides what you may do
They are the same thing with different names
Authorization happens before authentication
Authentication is for APIs, authorization is for web pages

questions.explanation: AuthN establishes identity (JWT, SSO, MFA). AuthZ evaluates that identity against policy for a specific action on a specific resource. A valid login must never imply permission.

questions.question: GET /invoices/1234 returns another customer's invoice when the id is changed to 1235. The user is logged in. What failed?

options.text: Object-level authorization (BOLA/IDOR) — ownership of the object was never checked
Authentication — the user was not logged in
Encryption — the invoice was not encrypted
Rate limiting — too many requests were allowed

questions.explanation: BOLA is OWASP API #1: the handler verified login but never asked whether this subject may read that object. A PDP check on (subject, read, invoice:1235) would deny it.

questions.question: An analyst for tenant A can read tenant B's rows because a query omitted the tenant predicate. What is the structural fix?

options.text: Enforce tenant isolation in policy (deny unless token tenant == resource tenant), tested in CI
Add more database indexes
Require a longer password
Cache the query results

questions.explanation: Tenant isolation is an authorization invariant, not a query-writing discipline. It belongs in centrally evaluated policy with tests, so one forgotten WHERE clause cannot leak a tenant.

questions.question: Your authorizer cannot reach the policy engine (timeout). What is the safe behavior?

options.text: Deny the request (fail closed) and alert
Allow the request so users are not blocked
Retry forever until the engine responds
Allow reads but deny writes

questions.explanation: Fail-closed is the load-bearing rule of authorization infrastructure. Fail-open turns every outage or misconfiguration into a breach. Timeouts, unknown inputs, and missing attributes must all resolve to DENY.

questions.question: Which statement best describes policy-based access control?

options.text: Authorization logic lives in versioned, testable policies evaluated by a PDP; apps enforce the decision
Every service hard-codes its own if-statements for speed
Access is granted once at login and never re-checked
Policies are written in emails and enforced by managers

questions.explanation: PBAC = externalize the decision (PDP + policy-as-code), keep enforcement in the app (PEP). Decisions are consistent, reviewable, testable, and auditable across all services.

questions.question: A mobile app calls GET /orders/{id} with the user's own JWT and returns other users' orders. The root-cause fix?

options.text: Server-side ownership check (subject vs order.owner) on every read
Longer, unguessable order IDs
Hiding the endpoint from API docs
Requiring re-login per request

questions.explanation: Unpredictable IDs are obscurity, not authorization. Only a per-request ownership decision closes BOLA.

questions.question: Your PDP client library throws on malformed responses. Where should that exception be caught?

options.text: At the PEP boundary — deny plus alert, never propagate into allow
In the UI toast notification
Nowhere — crash the process instead
In the metrics pipeline only

questions.explanation: Exception paths are decision paths. An unhandled throw that skips enforcement is fail-open by accident.

questions.question: Why do policies live in Git rather than a wiki page?

options.text: Review, versioning, tests, and automated deploy — the same lifecycle as code
Git is free file storage
Wikis cannot hold text
Auditors prefer markdown aesthetics

questions.explanation: Policy-as-code earns its name from the lifecycle: reviewed, tested, versioned, shipped — not the file format.
